summary: Defines how a SIP server acting as a PBX can register with a service provider for many phone numbers at once, so the provider can send calls for them to the PBX. It updates RFC 3680 and is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: An office phone system tells the phone company all its numbers in one go so every call is sent to it.

questions: sip pbx registration multiple phone numbers
what is the gin option tag in sip
what does the bnc parameter do in sip
how does a sip pbx register multiple phone numbers
subtitle: How a SIP-PBX tells its phone provider about a whole block of phone numbers with one REGISTER request.

tldr.problem: A small SIP-PBX has no static IP address and no reliable DNS name, yet its service provider must know where to send calls for every phone number the PBX serves. Registering each number separately is wasteful.
tldr.mechanism: The PBX sends one REGISTER request whose Contact URI carries a bnc parameter and no user part. The provider's registrar expands it into one binding per phone number the PBX owns, and the request is tagged with the gin option tag so that only servers that understand it handle it.
tldr.outcome: Calls to any of the PBX's numbers are forwarded to the PBX at the address it registered. The RFC also defines how this works with GRUUs, the registration event package, outbound connections and Path.

facts.label: Failure response for bnc plus user part

today: RFC 6140 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2011. It updates RFC 3680 by allowing a registration event subscriber to create multiple dialogs from one subscription request. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem of Bulk Registration
sections.content:
SIP was designed so that each user's Address of Record (AOR) is handled by the authority named in the AOR, and each user registers their own reachability information there. In real deployments some servers must receive calls for large blocks of AORs, and keeping a separate registration for each one is inefficient.

The RFC admits that using a REGISTER request to update many users at once goes somewhat beyond the original semantics in RFC 3261, but notes that the approach had already seen significant deployment. Small to medium SIP-PBX servers addressed by E.164 phone numbers use it to avoid maintaining DNS entries or static IP addresses. Two constraints drive the design: the SIP-PBX cannot be assumed to have a static IP address, and no DNS entry can be relied upon to resolve to it.

Because SIP URIs whose user part is an E.164 number are globally unique regardless of domain, the document focuses on registering such phone-number AORs.
sections.eli5: An office has hundreds of phone extensions, and its address keeps changing. Telling the phone company about each extension one by one would take forever, so there needs to be a shortcut.

sections.title: How the Mechanism Works
sections.content:
The mechanism is a REGISTER request with a specially formatted Contact URI. The URI carries the bnc parameter (bulk number contact), which says it stands for many phone-number contacts rather than one. A new option tag, gin (generate implicit numbers), lets a registrar and any intermediaries confirm they understand the mechanism.

Apart from this, the registrar handles the request normally, by adding AOR-to-Contact bindings to its location service. The list of AORs belonging to a SIP-PBX is a matter of local provisioning at the provider (the SSP) and at the PBX. The mechanism cannot detect or repair a mismatch, although the registration event package can be used to audit the AORs.
sections.eli5: The PBX sends one special note with a secret code word on it. The phone company sees the code word and knows to apply the note to every number it has on file for that office.

sections.title: Registering and Expanding Numbers
sections.content:
The SIP-PBX's REGISTER MUST contain the option tag gin in both a Require and a Proxy-Require header field. At least one Contact URI MUST carry the bnc parameter and MUST NOT have a user portion (no @). That URI may carry other parameters, which the SSP echoes back in requests bound for the PBX, except the user parameter, which is forbidden. The PBX also MUST support Path (RFC 3327) and MUST list path in its Supported header field.

The registrar uses the To header field to identify the PBX and authenticates it, for example with SIP digest or mutual TLS. It then stores one binding per associated AOR. Each AOR has the form the SSP expects from outsiders, such as sip:+12145550102@ssp.example.com. Each contact is the registered URI with the bnc parameter removed and the E.164 number added as the user part, so sip:198.51.100.3:5060;bnc becomes sip:+12145550102@198.51.100.3:5060. The number is a + followed only by digits, with no separators such as dashes or parentheses.

Renewal, expiry and removal belong to the bulk contact. A request to de-register one implicitly registered AOR MUST NOT remove it from the bulk registration. A number may also be registered explicitly in the normal way, and that registration is refreshed independently. A registrar that sees bnc together with a user portion, or together with a user parameter, MUST NOT send a 2xx response, and can answer 400 (Bad Request).
sections.eli5: The phone company checks who is calling, then writes an entry for every office number pointing to the one address, and crosses out the code word. Cancelling one number alone does nothing; you must cancel the whole note.

sections.title: Handling Incoming Calls
sections.content:
Once the bindings exist, the SSP proxy and registrar act as usual. For an inbound request addressed to an E.164 number assigned to one of its customers, it sets the target to the registered contacts and forwards the request as in Section 16.6 of RFC 3261. An SSP using this mechanism MUST do this for INVITE requests and for SUBSCRIBE requests to the reg event package, and SHOULD do it for all other methods, including unrecognized ones.

The SIP-PBX MUST NOT reject a request addressed to a bulk-registered number because the Request URI has a user parameter, lacks one, or has some particular value for it.
sections.eli5: When someone dials one of the office numbers, the phone company looks it up and passes the call to the office's address.

sections.title: Working with GRUU, Events, Outbound and Path
sections.content:
GRUUs. Public GRUU support is OPTIONAL. If the PBX invokes GRUU procedures for a bnc contact, the SSP assigns a public GRUU that also has a bnc parameter and no user portion. The PBX gives its own UAs a public GRUU made by adding an sg parameter, a token it can use to find the right device. When the SSP re-targets such a GRUU to the bulk contact, it MUST copy the sg parameter to the new target.

Registration events. Support for the registration event package of RFC 3680 is not required, but if present it must follow this RFC. Subscribing at the PBX's main URI yields one record per AOR. The SSP MUST proxy a reg SUBSCRIBE for a bulk-registered AOR to the PBX unless it holds complete, accurate and current data. As an explicit change to RFC 3680, a subscriber MAY create multiple dialogs from a single subscription request.

Outbound and Path. Client-initiated connections (RFC 5626) generally work unchanged, but the instance ID identifies the PBX itself, not its UAs. Path support is required in all SSPs and SIP-PBXes. All bindings from one bulk contact share a single path, and all AORs registered in one request share a common service route.
sections.eli5: The special note still works with the phone company's other features. A few details change, such as all numbers sharing one route, but they keep working together.

sections.title: Temporary GRUUs
sections.content:
Temporary GRUUs give privacy, so two of them must not reveal that they come from behind the same PBX. The SSP SHOULD support them. The SSP keeps an asymmetric key pair: K_e1 stays secret and K_e2 is given to PBXes through provisioning. In every successful REGISTER response the SSP puts a fixed-length, unforgeable temp-gruu-cookie parameter on each bnc Contact. The cookie stays the same for the whole registration, including refreshes.

For each temporary GRUU, the PBX makes a random distinguisher D (80 bits or longer is RECOMMENDED), encrypts the decoded cookie joined with D using K_e2, adds an HMAC keyed with its own secret, and builds a user part starting with tgruu.. The SSP decrypts with K_e1, checks the cookie and finds the right PBX registration. The PBX checks its own HMAC and uses the gr parameter to find the UA. A new temporary GRUU MUST be generated for every registration or refresh from a GRUU-supporting UA.
sections.eli5: The phone company gives each office a sealed envelope that only the phone company can open. The office puts its own random code inside, so no outsider can tell two disguised addresses came from the same office.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This is described as an unprecedented extension of REGISTER to more than one AOR, so a proxy might apply policy to the PBX named in To without knowing many AORs are involved. The Proxy-Require: gin header field solves this: proxies that do not understand the mechanism will not process the request.

Sharing a Path or Service-Route token among all AORs of one registration means the same policy applies to all of them, and proxy designers must avoid leaking sensitive information. Because outbound connections become shared between users, the PBX is the only entity able to hijack calls, and it must be trusted anyway.

The list of every number on a PBX can be sensitive, so SSPs are advised to use explicit white-list policies with conservative defaults. For temporary GRUUs, the HMAC choice is left to implementations. The RFC cites guidance of 2048-bit RSA keys for data needing protection through 2030 and 3072 bits after that. RSA decryption may amplify denial-of-service attacks, so rate limiting is suggested. Systems MUST make it easy to update the public key. The SSP SHOULD keep the retired key for a grace period, while PBXes MUST discard the old public key immediately.
sections.eli5: Letting one note cover many numbers could confuse helpers who only know about single numbers, so the note carries a warning label. The list of office numbers is private, so it should only be shown to people who are allowed.
